summary: Describes a simpler way for a SIP phone to turn an Alert-Info URN into a signal such as a ringtone. The alert URN namespace tells the phone the characteristics of a call, and the phone must pick a matching sound or behavior. This memo offers an easier method than the earlier one.

eli5.summary: A phone gets a note saying what kind of call this is, like urgent or doorbell. This explains an easier way to pick the right ring sound from that note.

questions: how phones pick ringtone from alert urn
finite state machine for signal selection
subtitle: Using finite state machines to resolve SIP alert URNs to ring tones

tldr.problem: RFC 7462 defines a large set of Alert-Info URNs that tell a phone what kind of call it is (urgent, internal, external, recall), but RFC 7462's algorithm for selecting which ring tone to play is complex and slow.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8433 offers an alternative: the phone's designer constructs a finite state machine offline, mapping URN symbols to states and states to ring tones. At runtime, each URN causes a state transition, and the final state determines the ring tone.
tldr.outcome: Phones can resolve alert URNs much faster and use less memory, while still satisfying RFC 7462 requirements. The approach is practical for embedded systems and UAs that customize their signals based on user preference.

today: RFC 8433 is an Informational RFC that proposes an alternative implementation method to RFC 7462. It has not obsoleted or updated RFC 7462, so both algorithms remain valid. VoIP implementations that need efficient, lightweight Signal selection can use the FSM approach. The RFC is particularly useful for embedded SIP UAs and systems where runtime efficiency and memory use are constrained.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP phones use the Alert-Info header field in INVITE requests and responses to signal information about the call to the user agent. The Alert-Info values can be URNs in the alert namespace that describe call characteristics: urn:alert:source:external for calls from outside the company, urn:alert:priority:high for urgent calls, urn:alert:service:recall for callbacks, and many others. RFC 7462 defines these URN categories and a resolution algorithm that selects which ring tone or ring back tone a phone should produce.

RFC 7462's algorithm is non-normative and can be complex: the phone must process URNs left to right, try to find signals that express each URN, and backtrack when a combination is not available. RFC 8433 proposes a simpler approach: design the finite state machine (FSM) offline based on the phone's actual signals and URNs, then use the FSM at runtime. The FSM approach is faster, uses less memory, and guarantees compliance with RFC 7462 requirements.
sections.eli5: Phones need to pick a ring tone based on notes about the call. Instead of thinking through a complex process each time, build a simple decision tree once and then just follow it.

sections.title: The Finite State Machine Approach
sections.content:
The FSM approach consists of three steps, performed once at design time. First, the designer lists the phone's signals (ring tones) and the set of alert URNs each signal should express. For example, one signal expresses urn:alert:source:internal, another expresses urn:alert:priority:high, and a third expresses both. Second, the designer maps all possible Alert-Info URNs into a finite alphabet of symbols. Each symbol corresponds to a relevant URN or category. For instance, the symbols might be Source:Internal, Source:External, Source:Other (for unknown sources), Priority:High, Priority:Low, and Priority:Other. Third, the designer constructs an FSM where each state represents the information extracted so far from the Alert-Info URNs, and each state has a corresponding signal.

At runtime, the phone simply initializes the FSM to its initial state (which corresponds to no alert information). For each URN in Alert-Info, the phone maps it to a symbol and executes the FSM transition for that symbol. The final state after processing all URNs determines which signal to render.
sections.eli5: Make a list of your ring tones and what each one means. Then make a simple table of states and transitions—like a flowchart where each URN moves you to the next state. When a call comes in, just follow the flowchart.

sections.title: Constructing the Finite State Machine
sections.content:
The FSM construction uses a straightforward process. Start by listing all relevant URN categories (such as source, priority, and service) by examining which URNs the phone's signals express. Next, partition the infinite space of possible URNs into a finite alphabet of symbols. For the source category, symbols might be Source (no specific source), Source:Internal, Source:External, and Source:Other (unknown or unsupported sources). Symbols also include ancestor URNs created by removing trailing components—for instance, the symbol Source is the ancestor of Source:Internal and Source:External.

Then construct the states and transitions. Each state is labeled by a set of symbols (one per relevant category) representing the information accumulated from URNs processed so far. The initial state has null symbols for all categories. Each state has a corresponding signal (the one that best expresses the state's label). Transitions are computed by combining the input symbol with the current state's symbol for that category, following semantic precedence rules from RFC 7462: if the input symbol is more specific (a longer URN), prefer it; if not, keep the current state's symbol.
sections.eli5: List your ring tones and what they mean. Figure out the categories that matter (like source and priority). For each combination of categories you might see, decide which ring tone to play. That combination becomes a state, and moving from one URN to the next is a state transition.

sections.title: Practical Examples
sections.content:
A simple example: a phone with three signals: default (no specific meaning), internal source (for urn:alert:source:internal), and external source (for urn:alert:source:external). The FSM has an initial state labeled Source (null source), which renders the default signal. When the phone receives urn:alert:source:internal, it transitions to state Source:Internal and renders the internal source signal. If it receives urn:alert:source:external from state Source:Internal, it stays in Source:Internal because the new URN is not compatible with the current state's signal (you cannot have both internal and external source).

A more complex example: a phone that can signal source (internal/external) and priority (high/low) in any combination. This creates 9 signals and an FSM with 16 states, where processing multiple URNs produces different results depending on order. For instance, receiving (internal, high priority) selects the internal-high-priority signal, but receiving (high priority, internal) with no internal-high-priority signal might select only high priority if the FSM's state transitions force a fallback. RFC 8433 provides detailed worked examples showing this behavior.
sections.eli5: If a phone has signals for internal calls, external calls, high priority, and low priority, each combination of (source, priority) is a different state. Some combinations might not have a signal, so you fall back to the closest one.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC provides a Python implementation of the FSM construction algorithm so designers do not have to build state machines by hand. The algorithm is sound: it automatically generates an FSM that conforms to RFC 7462's resolution requirements. For simple phones with few signals and URN categories, the FSM can be constructed by hand or ad hoc analysis. For phones with many signals and dynamic signal sets, automatic generation is essential. The RFC also discusses how to handle dynamic signal sets (if the user can customize ring tones) by either regenerating the FSM, using a generic FSM instantiated for the current signals, or computing states dynamically during Alert-Info processing.

Phones typically have two FSMs: one for processing Alert-Info in incoming INVITE requests (to select the ring tone) and one for processing Alert-Info in provisional responses (to select the ring back tone the caller hears). Both FSMs are constructed the same way but based on different lists of signals.
sections.eli5: The RFC includes code to build the state machine automatically. Some phones build it once at startup. Others let users change ring tones, so they rebuild when the user changes settings. A phone might have different FSMs for incoming calls and for what the caller hears.
